content.text:
Short answer you can use at lunch:
- "Scanned PDF" usually means an image-only PDF: each page is just a picture (a raster image) of the paper. There are no real text objects to select, copy, or index.
- "Searchable PDF" means the file contains real text data you can search/select/copy. That text either comes from the original digital source or was added by OCR; sometimes a scanned page is made searchable by adding a hidden text layer.

A bit more detail (concise, technical but clear):
- Inside a PDF, page content can be images or text drawing commands. A scanned/image PDF stores each page as an image XObject. A searchable PDF contains text drawing operations (operators like TJ/Tj) that encode actual character strings plus font info.
- OCRed/searchable scanned PDF: common pattern is a "sandwich" — the visible layer is the scanned image, and an invisible text layer (positioned to match the image) contains the recognized words. The text layer is what makes the file searchable.
- Native/digital PDF: generated from an application (Word, LaTeX) and contains proper text and fonts (vector/text objects) rather than page images.
- Accessibility: searchable text helps screen readers, but being searchable ≠ fully accessible. Properly tagged text and reading order are additional requirements for good accessibility.
- File-size/quality: image-only PDFs (especially high-res scans) tend to be larger. OCR adds small text data but usually not much size. Converting an image to vector text (i.e., original digital PDF) keeps smaller size and sharper text.

How to check quickly:
- Try to select text or copy/paste from the PDF. If you can, it’s searchable (or at least contains text).
- Search for a word in the PDF viewer. If it finds hits, there’s searchable text.
- Open in a plain text viewer (or run pdftotext). If you get readable text, it’s not purely image-based.

One-line analogy: a scanned PDF is a photograph of a page; a searchable PDF has actual words behind the picture (or no picture at all).
